summary: Explains how BGP can advertise IPv4 reachability information with an IPv6 next-hop address. Earlier rules tied the next-hop address family to the route's address family, which made this awkward, so the document defines how to signal and handle the combination, letting IPv4 routes run over an IPv6-only core.

eli5.summary: Imagine giving directions to a street in the old numbering system but saying the next step is a turn written in the new system. This explains how routers can understand that mix.

subtitle: How BGP can announce IPv4 routes whose next hop is an IPv6 address, so IPv4 can ride over an IPv6 core.

tldr.problem: The BGP address-family definitions for IPv4 routes only allow an IPv4 next-hop address, so there was no way to advertise IPv4 or VPN-IPv4 reachability through an IPv6 next hop.
tldr.mechanism: The next-hop field length tells the receiver which protocol the address belongs to (16 or 32 bytes means IPv6, 24 or 48 bytes means VPN-IPv6), and a BGP capability called Extended Next Hop Encoding lets peers agree to use it.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 islands and IPv4 VPNs can be connected across an IPv6 backbone, gradually and without a flag day. It obsoletes RFC 5549, changing the VPN next-hop encoding and adding multicast VPN support.

facts.label: Capability triple
facts.value: NLRI AFI, NLRI SAFI, Nexthop AFI (2 octets each)

today: RFC 8950 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2020. It obsoletes RFC 5549, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem: IPv4 Routes, IPv6 Next Hop
sections.content:
Multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP) decides which kinds of next-hop address are allowed by looking at the AFI (Address Family Identifier) and SAFI (Subsequent Address Family Identifier) of the routes being announced. The NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information) is the set of destinations being announced, and the next hop is the address of the router to send traffic to.

Carriers sometimes need to connect 'islands' of one address family across a transit core of another. That includes IPv4 islands across an IPv6 core. For IPv6 routes with an IPv4 next hop, solutions already existed (RFC 4798 and RFC 4659). For IPv4 routes, the definitions for <1/1>, <1/2>, <1/4>, <1/128> and <1/129> assume an IPv4 or VPN-IPv4 next hop, and the RFC says there is no generally applicable way to hide an IPv6 address inside the IPv4 field.

This document fills that gap. It extends the AFI/SAFI definitions, defines how the next-hop encoding reveals its protocol, and adds a BGP capability so peers can discover support dynamically. The capability allows gradual deployment without a flag day or any risk of traffic black-holing.
sections.eli5: Routers used to assume that if a street was written the old way, the next turn was too. This RFC says: the next turn may use the new writing, and here is how to tell.

sections.title: Changes Compared to RFC 5549
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 5549 and makes two significant changes.

  • For AFI/SAFI <1/128>, RFC 5549 encoded the next hop as an IPv6 address of 16 or 32 bytes. It is now encoded as a VPN-IPv6 address of 24 or 48 bytes. This matches how existing implementations behave and addresses Erratum ID 5253. The RFC states that all known and deployed implementations are interoperable and already use the new encoding, so the change does not break interoperability.
  • AFI/SAFI <1/129> (IPv4 multicast VPN) may now also use an IPv6 underlay, with encoding and procedures similar to <1/128>.
sections.eli5: This is a corrected edition. One label format was fixed to match what everyone already did, and one more kind of route was allowed.

sections.title: Extended Next Hop Encoding in MP_REACH_NLRI
sections.content:
The extension lives in the MP_REACH_NLRI attribute. For plain IPv4 routes (AFI 1, SAFI 1, 2 or 4), the Length of Next Hop Address is 16 or 32, and the address is an IPv6 address, optionally followed by the link-local IPv6 address of the next hop, built as in Section 3 of RFC 2545.

For VPN-IPv4 routes (AFI 1, SAFI 128 or 129), the length is 24 or 48 and the next hop is a VPN-IPv6 address with an 8-octet Route Distinguisher (RD) set to zero, optionally followed by the link-local VPN-IPv6 address, also with a zero RD.

The receiver MUST use the Length of Next Hop Address field to decide which protocol the next hop belongs to. This is the same method used in RFC 4684 and RFC 6074. The older behaviour (IPv4 next hop for IPv4 routes, VPN-IPv4 next hop for <1/128> and <1/129>) remains valid.
sections.eli5: The note carrying the next step has a length. A short note means the old address style, a longer one means the new style, and the router just measures it.

sections.title: The Extended Next Hop Encoding Capability
sections.content:
A speaker that wants to send IPv4 or VPN-IPv4 routes with an IPv6 next hop MUST first learn, through the capability mechanism of RFC 5492, that its peer supports the Extended Next Hop Encoding capability for that AFI/SAFI pair. Capability Code is 5. The Capability Value is a list of triples, each made of NLRI AFI (2 octets), NLRI SAFI (2 octets) and Nexthop AFI (2 octets).

This document only allows NLRI AFI 1 (IPv4), NLRI SAFI 1, 2, 4, 128 or 129, and Nexthop AFI 2 (IPv6). It is not meant for AFI/SAFIs that already allow both IPv4 and IPv6 next hops (such as <1/132>) or already have a solution (such as <2/1> with an IPv4 next hop). New AFI/SAFIs are expected to allow both next-hop types from the start.

The capability only says how the next hop is encoded. Whether an AFI/SAFI may be used at all between two peers is still decided purely by the Multiprotocol Extensions capability of RFC 4760.
sections.eli5: Before using the new style, two routers ask each other, 'Can you read this?' Only if both say yes do they use it.

sections.title: Operations and Usage Examples
sections.content:
By default, if a BGP session runs over IPvx and the speaker puts its own address in as the next hop, the next hop SHOULD be an IPvx address, using the encoding rules of the AFI/SAFI being updated. Policy may override this. When a next hop is passed along unchanged, as a Route Reflector does, its encoding MUST NOT be changed. If a route reflector client cannot handle that encoding, the NLRI cannot be distributed to it, so for sound routing all clients may need to handle every encoding any of them generates.

The RFC gives three usage examples. Address Family Border Routers (AFBRs) can interconnect IPv4 islands over an IPv6 backbone using <1/1>, as discussed in RFC 5565. PE routers can carry IPv4 VPN unicast over an IPv6 core with SAFI 128, and IPv4 multicast VPN with SAFI 129. In each case the PE routers advertise the capability with the matching <NLRI AFI=1, NLRI SAFI, Nexthop AFI=2> triple.
sections.eli5: Normally a router names itself using the same kind of address as the link it talks over. If it is just passing along someone else's directions, it must not rewrite them.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document defines no new code points. RFC 5549 had added Extended Next Hop Encoding to the Capability Codes registry with value 5, and IANA has updated the entry to refer to this document.

The RFC says it raises no additional security issues beyond BGP-4 and its Multiprotocol Extensions. It does note that BGP is vulnerable to traffic diversion attacks (RFC 4272), and that advertising an IPv6 next hop adds a new way to divert traffic. Traffic could be forwarded to a distant target across an intervening network such as an IPv6 core, so less infrastructure has to be subverted.

The IPv6 next hop could even be an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address (RFC 4291), and any next-hop security checks an operator has deployed need to account for that case.
sections.eli5: A sneaky router could point traffic to the wrong place using this too, so the usual BGP protections still matter, and checks have to understand the new address style.
